related_questions.question: What is diabetes mellitus type 2 type?
related_questions.snippet: Type 2 diabetes, the most common type of diabetes, is a disease that occurs when your blood glucose, also called blood sugar, is too high. Blood glucose is your main source of energy and comes mainly from the food you eat. Insulin, a hormone made by the pancreas, helps glucose get into your cells to be used for energy.
related_questions.title: Type 2 Diabetes - NIDDK

related_questions.question: How serious is type 2 diabetes mellitus?
related_questions.snippet: Over time, high blood sugar levels in type 2 diabetes can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart. This can happen because the pancreas doesn't make enough of a hormone called insulin that helps sugar enter the cells. It happens also because the cells respond poorly to insulin by taking in less sugar.
related_questions.title: Type 2 diabetes - Symptoms and causes - Mayo Clinic

related_questions.question: What is diabetes mellitus level 2?
related_questions.snippet: In type 2 diabetes, your body does not use insulin properly—this is called insulin resistance. At first, your beta cells make extra insulin to make up for it. Over time, your pancreas can't make enough insulin to keep your blood glucose at normal levels.
related_questions.title: Understanding Type 2 Diabetes | ADA

text_blocks.snippet: While many people with type 2 diabetes manage their condition with lifestyle changes and oral medications, some do eventually require insulin. Insulin is a hormone that helps regulate blood sugar levels, and type 2 diabetes occurs when the body doesn't use insulin properly or doesn't produce enough. Initially, lifestyle changes like diet and exercise, and oral medications like metformin, are often the first line of treatment. However, as type 2 diabetes progresses, the pancreas may not be able to produce enough insulin to keep blood sugar levels within a healthy range, necessitating insulin injections.
When is insulin needed for type 2 diabetes?

list.title: Progression of the disease:
list.snippet: As type 2 diabetes progresses, the body's ability to produce and utilize insulin can decline.

list.title: Ineffectiveness of other treatments:
list.snippet: If lifestyle changes and oral medications are no longer effective in managing blood sugar levels, insulin may be added to the treatment plan.

list.title: Specific situations:
list.snippet: In some cases, such as during pregnancy or during periods of illness or stress, insulin may be needed temporarily.

list.title: Individualized treatment:
list.snippet: The need for insulin varies from person to person, and the decision to start insulin therapy is made by a healthcare professional based on individual needs and circumstances.

text_blocks.snippet: Types of insulin used in type 2 diabetes:

list.snippet: Long-acting insulin: Provides a steady background level of insulin to help control blood sugar throughout the day.
Rapid-acting or short-acting insulin: Used before meals to help control blood sugar spikes after eating.
Intermediate-acting insulin: Provides longer-lasting coverage than rapid-acting insulin.
Premixed insulin: Combines different types of insulin in one injection to simplify dosing.

list.title: Individualized treatment:
list.snippet: It's crucial to work with a healthcare professional to determine the best insulin regimen for your specific needs.

list.title: Education and monitoring:
list.snippet: People using insulin should be educated on how to properly administer it, monitor their blood sugar levels, and manage potential side effects like hypoglycemia (low blood sugar).

list.title: Preventing complications:
list.snippet: Effective blood sugar control with insulin, along with other lifestyle modifications, can help prevent or delay the serious long-term complications of diabetes, such as eye problems, kidney disease, and nerve damage.

text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a condition where the body either doesn't produce enough insulin or can't properly use the insulin it produces, leading to high blood sugar levels. It's often linked to lifestyle factors like diet, exercise, and weight, and is more common in middle-aged and older adults, though it's increasingly seen in younger individuals.
snippet_highlighted_words: a condition where the body either doesn't produce enough insulin or can't properly use the insulin it produces, leading to high blood sugar levels

list.title: Insulin Resistance:
list.snippet: The body's cells become resistant to insulin, meaning they don't respond effectively to the hormone's signal to take up glucose from the bloodstream.

list.title: Pancreas Function:
list.snippet: Initially, the pancreas may try to compensate by producing more insulin, but over time, it may not be able to keep up with the demand.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Common symptoms include increased thirst and urination, increased hunger, fatigue, blurred vision, and slow-healing sores. Some people may not experience any noticeable symptoms.

list.title: Risk Factors:
list.snippet: Being overweight or obese, having a family history of diabetes, being physically inactive, and belonging to certain ethnic groups (like African Americans, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Asian American, and Pacific Islander) are risk factors, according to the American Diabetes Association.

list.title: Complications:
list.snippet: Type 2 diabetes can lead to serious complications, including heart and blood vessel disease, nerve damage (neuropathy), kidney disease (diabetic nephropathy), eye damage (diabetic retinopathy), skin conditions, and slow healing.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Blood tests like the A1C test or glucose tolerance test can diagnose type 2 diabetes.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Management involves lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, weight loss), oral medications, and sometimes insulin therapy.

list.title: Early Detection:
list.snippet: Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent or delay complications.

list.title: Individualized Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment plans are tailored to each individual's needs and may change over time.

list.title: Lifelong Condition:
list.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition that requires ongoing management, though some individuals may achieve remission with significant lifestyle changes.
